en.title: Clayface Film Unleashes Universal Monsters Vibe on DCU
en.summary: Get ready for a darker, gooier take on a classic Batman villain. The upcoming **Clayface** film promises a body horror spectacle steeped in the atmospheric dread of old-school monster movies.
en.body:
Forget capes and laser eyes for a moment; the DC Universe is diving headfirst into the chilling embrace of classic horror with its upcoming **Clayface** film. Scheduled for release on October 23, 2026, this project is poised to be the first true horror entry in the new DCU slate, Chapter One: Gods and Monsters, and it’s bringing a distinct **Universal Monsters** sensibility back to Gotham.

The film, directed by **James Watkins** and penned by **Mike Flanagan** and **Hossein Amini**, taps into the character's origins, which, while not initially supernatural, were intrinsically linked to the pulp sensibilities of early monster cinema. The original **Clayface**, Basil Karlo, debuted in 1940, a year that saw a surge in horror films from Universal Pictures. This new iteration, however, moves beyond the mask-wearing actor of the past, opting for a more contemporary, yet equally terrifying, body horror origin story.

## A New Kind of Monsterpiece

Instead of a simple B-movie actor, the film’s **Matt Hagen**, portrayed by **Tom Rhys Harries**, is an actor who achieves critical acclaim but finds himself entangled in the dangerous underworld of Gotham. The narrative kicks off with Hagen nervously awaiting nominations for an award, only to face brutal consequences after a celebratory incident angers a local gangster. This sets the stage for his transformation, hinting at a descent into shapeshifting chaos that echoes the tragic, monstrous figures of yesteryear. The review notes that while this **Clayface** isn't aiming for the iconic heights of **Bride of Frankenstein** or **The Invisible Man**, it certainly aims to capture the spirit of sequels like **The Invisible Man Returns** or **The Mummy's Hand** – films that, while perhaps less prestigious, offered potent doses of creature-feature thrills.

## Fan Frenzy: Body Horror Meets Gotham Grit

Fans of the DC Universe and horror aficionados alike are buzzing about this unique blend. The prospect of a DC film leaning heavily into body horror, a subgenre famously explored by directors like David Cronenberg, is particularly exciting. This isn't just another superhero flick; it's a deep dive into the psychological and physical disintegration of a character, presented through a lens that respects the atmospheric dread and character-driven terror of the original **Universal Monsters**. The decision to ground the film in a pulp world where celebrity, crime, and monstrous transformation collide offers a fresh narrative approach that promises to resonate with viewers seeking more than just spectacle. The anticipation is palpable for how **Watkins**, **Flanagan**, and **Amini** will translate this ambitious vision to the screen.

What's Next

With **Clayface** set to be one of the first major releases under Skydance Corporation's new deal with Warner Bros. Pictures, all eyes are on its October 23, 2026 release date. Fans will be watching closely for any further casting announcements and glimpses into the visual style that will define this monstrous new addition to the DCU.

content_raw: The original incarnation of the Batman villain Clayface first appeared in the summer of 1940, with the name Basil Karlo as an homage to a pair of genre-movie actors. That tribute was particularly important because the character was not yet made of clay or in possession of shapeshifting abilities, as he would be in later versions; he was just a B-movie actor using a clay mask to assume the identity of Karlo’s former horror-movie character. Even without the aid of the supernatural, however, Clayface was a natural fit for that year, which saw the release of no fewer than three Universal Monster movies, as sequels to The Invisible Man and The Mummy joined a second wave of monster cinema that would continue for the remainder of the decade. The new film version of Clayface does not feature a mask-wearing Basil Karlo. Like some of the character’s later iterations in different media, it mixes and matches a few different comics elements, keeping the acting we’re not talking about a James Whale-level monsterpiece like Bride Of Frankenstein or The Invisible Man . But The Invisible Man Returns or The Mummy’s Hand ? Sure, Clayface can live up to that.  Hagen has his eye on greater prestige, however. As the movie opens, he’s nervously awaiting news of Oscar nominations (or their DCU equivalent), then basking in his relief and elation upon finding out that he’s among the five Best Actor honorees. When he celebrates in his hometown of Gotham City, however, he accidentally angers gangster Markos Szabo (David Dencik), and receives a facial slashing for his trouble—the first sign that despite a nominally contemporary setting, this movie will be rooted firmly in a pulp world where it’s not only possible for the mafia to slice up a handsome celebrity with impunity, but for the gangsters to somehow plant enough negative rumors in the press that it’s the cracked actor who comes out of the situation looking like the bad guy. (In a nicely noirish touch, it’s never fully specified what those stories about Hagen’s hardscrabble Gotham youth are, or whether they’re actually true. The vague implication is that they probably are.) After some unsuccessful attempts at reconstructive surgery and a career time-out in Gotham, a heavily scarred Hagen tracks down Caitlyn Corr (Naomie Ackie), a scientist perilously close to losing the funding to experiment with her breakthrough nano-cell technology, which somehow involves using microscopic A.I. to rebuilt damaged tissue. Hagen aggressively volunteers his body to test her work, and despite the potential legal messiness, the prospect of an enthusiastic human subject is too much for her to resist. She’s also drawn to Hagen himself, and the movie makes their maybe-pairing both less likely and less unappealing by handing Caitlyn a working-stiff cop fiancé (Max Minghella), a character with classic (and classically dull) monster-movie functionality.
